A second investigator, starting fresh with the same tools, tested the kind of each fault in your draft answer. Their findings:

### `ts-preserve-service`: you said `http_aborted`. They conclude `network_partition` (confidence: low).
Scope: Only ts-preserve-service's calls to ts-order-service on POST /api/v1/orderservice/order fail: 474 of 474 such Client spans in the incident, against none in normal. The callee's Server spans for those same calls return 200 at normal latency, and order's other callers (seat POST, security GET, ui-dashboard refresh) see no errors. Preserve's calls to travel, basic, seat, contacts and security are unaffected, and both pods keep emitting spans, logs and metrics. Whether other routes on the preserve-to-order connection are spared cannot be tested, because that pair carries only POST /order in the traces.
Ruled out:
- `http_aborted`: The lead's claim is weakened. The caller's error is a socket-level 'Unexpected end of file from server' (java.net.SocketException), which is a TCP-level close rather than an application-level HTTP cut. The callee's Server span records a normal 200 for all 474 failed calls, so no abort appears on the server side. The fault is also confined to one pod pair, and the data cannot show it is confined to one route on that connection.
- `http_wrong_status_code`: The callee returns 200 on every failed call and the caller reports no status mismatch; the failure is a socket EOF, not a wrong status.
- `http_response_body_corrupted`: There is no parse or content error in the caller's logs; the failure is a socket-level EOF, and the callee's 200 spans show no diverging content signal.
- `pod_unavailable`: Order keeps emitting spans (1,809 to 3,584 per minute) and logs (665 to 1,280 per minute), and its metric rows stay at 317 per minute. Its other callers succeed, so the instance is not gone.
- `pod_failure`: No restart or uptime reset appears for order or preserve, and the callee answers 200 on the failed calls, so there was no kill-and-restart gap.
- `dns_lookup_failed`: The error text is an I/O error after connection (Unexpected end of file), with no UnknownHost or name-resolution text.
- `network_delay`: The failed calls are not slow. Their p50 is 6.5 ms and p95 8.9 ms, close to normal, and the minimum is 1.8 ms. Delay would move every call, not produce an error.
- `network_loss`: Not separable from network_partition under the equivalence rule; the failures are fast EOFs with no retransmit tail near 200 ms, so loss with 100 percent failure fits the partition shape better. Both are the same answer for scoring.
- `network_corrupt`: Corruption would surface as deserialization or checksum errors below the application. The caller shows a socket EOF instead, and the callee's own 200 responses are not corrupted.
- `database_call_failed`: The failed calls are HTTP POSTs to order, not database statements, and the error is at the socket level rather than from a SQL layer.
- `application_exception`: Order's server spans show no error status on any POST /order call (0 errors), so the exception is not in order's application code.

ruled_out.why: The lead's claim is weakened. The caller's error is a socket-level 'Unexpected end of file from server' (java.net.SocketException), which is a TCP-level close rather than an application-level HTTP cut. The callee's Server span records a normal 200 for all 474 failed calls, so no abort appears on the server side. The fault is also confined to one pod pair, and the data cannot show it is confined to one route on that connection.
The callee returns 200 on every failed call and the caller reports no status mismatch; the failure is a socket EOF, not a wrong status.
There is no parse or content error in the caller's logs; the failure is a socket-level EOF, and the callee's 200 spans show no diverging content signal.
Order keeps emitting spans (1,809 to 3,584 per minute) and logs (665 to 1,280 per minute), and its metric rows stay at 317 per minute. Its other callers succeed, so the instance is not gone.
No restart or uptime reset appears for order or preserve, and the callee answers 200 on the failed calls, so there was no kill-and-restart gap.
The error text is an I/O error after connection (Unexpected end of file), with no UnknownHost or name-resolution text.
The failed calls are not slow. Their p50 is 6.5 ms and p95 8.9 ms, close to normal, and the minimum is 1.8 ms. Delay would move every call, not produce an error.

Not separable from network_partition under the equivalence rule; the failures are fast EOFs with no retransmit tail near 200 ms, so loss with 100 percent failure fits the partition shape better. Both are the same answer for scoring.
Corruption would surface as deserialization or checksum errors below the application. The caller shows a socket EOF instead, and the callee's own 200 responses are not corrupted.
The failed calls are HTTP POSTs to order, not database statements, and the error is at the socket level rather than from a SQL layer.
Order's server spans show no error status on any POST /order call (0 errors), so the exception is not in order's application code.

**Verdict: the evidence does not support `http_aborted` for `ts-preserve-service`. It fits a transport-level cut on the preserve→order connection better (`network_partition`, which is in the same equivalence class as `network_loss`). Confidence is low, because the telemetry has no second route on that connection to test for route-specificity.**

**What the lead's evidence shows, checked:**
- All 474 preserve→order POST calls fail (474 of 474 Client spans in the incident, 0 normal). Order's Server spans for those same calls all return 200, with p50 6.5 ms. Those are real successes on the order side.
- The caller's error text is `Unexpected end of file from server` / `java.net.SocketException`. That is a socket-level close seen by the client, not an HTTP-level error or status. The `http_aborted` definition explicitly contrasts with a TCP-level disconnect.
- The failures are fast, not hung. The failed calls have p50 6.5 ms, min 1.8 ms and p95 8.9 ms, close to the normal range. Only 3 of 477 errored Client spans have no Server child.

**Scope and the other calls:**
- Preserve's other calls, to travel, basic, seat, contacts, security and food (GET and POST), are all error-free, with latencies roughly flat. The fault is confined to one pair of pods.
- Order's other callers are error-free in the incident: seat POST (1,565 calls), security GET (478), ui-dashboard POST `/order/refresh` (23). Order itself is alive, with span and log volume rising, not falling.
- In the traces, the preserve→order connection carries only POST `/order`. So I could not test whether other routes on that connection are spared, which is the main thing that would separate `http_aborted` (route-specific) from a connection-level network fault. Absence of other traffic on that pair means this cannot be settled from the data.

**Against `network_*` as well:**
- Hubble drop counters show no drops attributable to the preserve→order pair. Drops are small and spread across many pods. Flows on that pair keep counting at high volume. That weakens a hard partition, but it doesn't rule one out.
- The failures are fast EOFs, not timeouts. A partition that "fails at once" usually shows connect or reset errors, not EOF after a 200. So the transport story is also imperfect.

**Net:** the failure is a 100% socket-level EOF on one pod pair, while the callee records a successful 200 and everything else on the caller is healthy. Read literally, the `http_aborted` definition (an application-level cut, not a TCP-level disconnect) fits this poorly. The lead's own evidence (callee 200) argues against an HTTP-level abort, since an abort would usually show up at the server span. The best-supported class is the network-blocking class on the preserve→order link. The data cannot cleanly separate that from an HTTP abort on the POST route, so treat this as a low-confidence rejection of `http_aborted`, not a confirmed alternative.
